title: The road to Emmaus (Luke 24:13–35)
hook: two sad friends walk seven miles with a stranger and know him in the breaking of bread

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mary Magdalene in the garden: she took him for the gardener until he said her name, and she answered, Rabboni. Your line was he says your name. Now, the walk home.

Same Sunday, late afternoon. Two of Jesus's followers are walking home from Jerusalem to a village called Emmaus, sixty furlongs away, Luke says, about seven miles. One is named Cleophas. The other, Luke never names. They go over it again and again, the way people do on the long drive home from a funeral. A stranger falls into step beside them and asks what they're talking about. They stop. Their faces fall. Are you the only visitor in Jerusalem who hasn't heard? Then the words that give it all away: we had hoped he was the one. Had hoped. Past tense.
screen: `SEVEN MILES, WALKING HOME.` → `A STRANGER FALLS INTO STEP.` → `WE HAD HOPED.`

segments.voice: The stranger is Jesus, but Luke says their eyes were held so they didn't know him. He doesn't reveal himself. He walks with them and opens the Scriptures, from Moses through all the prophets, showing how the Messiah had to suffer and so enter his glory. Seven miles of Bible study. At the village he acts as if he's going further, and they beg him, in the Douay-Rheims: "Stay with us, because it is towards evening, and the day is now far spent." He goes in. At the table he takes the bread, blesses it, breaks it and gives it to them: the same four movements as the Last Supper. Their eyes are opened, they know him, and he vanishes. They turn to each other: "Was not our heart burning within us, whilst he spoke in the way, and opened to us the scriptures?" That same hour, Luke says, they walk the seven miles back, to tell the others how they knew him "in the breaking of bread." The Catechism sees the shape of the Mass in this road. First the Word: the Scriptures read and opened. Then the table: bread taken, blessed, broken, given. Two parts, in the order Luke tells it. And notice where he's recognized. Not in the explaining, as good as it was. In the bread. Pope John Paul II named a letter on the Eucharist after their plea: stay with us, Lord.
screen: `THEIR EYES WERE HELD.` · `SEVEN MILES OF SCRIPTURE.` · `TOOK, BLESSED, BROKE, GAVE.` · `THE WORD, THEN THE TABLE: THE MASS.` · then, large: `WAS NOT OUR HEART BURNING WITHIN US?`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone whose hope has gone into the past tense lately, we had hoped, I used to think, and picture yourself falling into step beside them. You don't need the right words: the stranger started with a question and let them talk, so think of one question you could ask, and then just listen. If you pray, you can ask to be good company on someone's road.
Emmaus. The village seven miles off, where two sad friends finally recognized Jesus in the breaking of the bread.
Your line: was not our heart burning. They knew him in the breaking of bread. Day sixty-nine, done.

howItsDone: Catholics hear the Emmaus story in the Easter season, and the Catechism sees in it the two parts of every Mass: the Liturgy of the Word and the Liturgy of the Eucharist.

original.note: Greek: the breaking of the bread. Acts uses the same phrase for what the first believers did together.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about a walk.
what it means: two people who've lost hope are met on the road, have the Scriptures opened, and recognize him at the table.
what a scholar hears: took, blessed, broke, gave: the Last Supper's four verbs. the Word, then the bread, the shape Catholics find in every Mass.

notes: Douay-Rheims wording of Luke 24:29, 24:32 and 24:35 given from memory; confirm (e.g. 'whilst' and 'the scriptures' lowercase).
Distance: the Douay-Rheims says 'sixty furlongs'; about seven miles. Some manuscripts read 160 furlongs. The location of Emmaus is uncertain (several sites claimed).
CCC 1347 draws the Emmaus parallel to the Mass (Liturgy of the Word, Liturgy of the Eucharist). Confirm reference.
Mane Nobiscum Domine, apostolic letter of John Paul II for the Year of the Eucharist, 7 October 2004. Confirm.
Greek κλάσις τοῦ ἄρτου (Acts 2:42; Luke 24:35 has the dative ἐν τῇ κλάσει τοῦ ἄρτου). Confirm spelling and transliteration.
